To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
radiotherapy is an effective treatment option for localized prostate cancer.
radiotherapy for prostate carcinoma without lymph node invasion is effective for low- and intermediate-risk patients and that the outcome is not so good for high-risk patients.

the outcome of patients with localized prostate cancer treated by radiotherapy after confirming the absence of lymph node invasion depends on the initial and nadir PSA, advanced stage and PSA doubling time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the outcome of prostate cancer patients who had lymph node-negative status.
the management of lymph nodes in prostate cancer.
the outcome of prostate cancer patients treated by radiotherapy after lymphadenectomy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lymph nodes were not a major issue for failure.
radiotherapy is an effective treatment for patients with localized prostate cancer and negative nodes.
lymph node invasion was not the only cause of treatment failure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer is effective, but the treatment strategy should be different depending on risk group.
the absence of lymph nodes in prostate cancer does not influence outcome in radiotherapy.
the absence of lymph node invasion does not necessarily indicate a good outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that

patients with low and intermediate risks of prostate cancer do not need to be treated with hormone therapy immediately following radiotherapy, but rather can be monitored for recurrence and hormone therapy can be initiated at the time of recurrence.
patients with localized prostate cancer and negative lymph node invasion treated with radiotherapy have good outcomes, and that hormone therapy should be administered after failure, not before.
lymph nodes do not play a role for the treatment outcome.
